energy-diagrams-s1.title: Energy diagram for a gas-phase reaction
energy-diagrams-s1.text: The diagram shows the enthalpy of a reacting system as the reaction X(g) + Y(g) → Z(g) proceeds, per mole of reaction. The three marked levels are: reactants 125 kJ, top of the hump 214 kJ, products 38 kJ.

energy-diagrams-s2.title: Readings from four energy diagrams
energy-diagrams-s2.text: A student reads three levels from the energy diagrams of four reactions, each per mole of reaction.

table.caption: Enthalpy levels read from each diagram

items.q: Use the diagram to determine ΔH for the reaction X + Y → Z, in kJ/mol.

mistakes.why: Sign: you subtracted products from reactants. ΔH is products minus reactants, and the products here are lower, so ΔH is negative.
Value: that is the activation energy, the climb from the reactants to the peak. ΔH compares the two flat ends.

why.correct: ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) = 38 kJ − 125 kJ = −87 kJ per mole of reaction. Products sit below reactants, so the sign is negative.

items.q: Use the diagram to determine the activation energy of the forward reaction, in kJ/mol.

mistakes.why: Value: you measured from the products to the peak, which is the activation energy of the reverse reaction.
Value: you read the height of the peak. The activation energy is the climb from the reactants up to the peak.

why.correct: Ea(forward) = H(peak) − H(reactants) = 214 kJ − 125 kJ = 89 kJ/mol.

items.q: Which statement about the reverse reaction, Z → X + Y, is supported by the diagram?
options: It is exothermic, with ΔH = −87 kJ/mol and an activation energy of 89 kJ/mol.
It is endothermic, with ΔH = +87 kJ/mol and an activation energy of 89 kJ/mol.
It is endothermic, with ΔH = +87 kJ/mol and an activation energy of 176 kJ/mol.
It is endothermic, with ΔH = +87 kJ/mol and an activation energy of zero.

why.correct: For the reverse reaction, ΔH = 125 − 38 = +87 kJ/mol and Ea(reverse) = 214 − 38 = 176 kJ/mol. The diagram is read right to left.
options: This copies the forward values. Reversing the direction flips the sign of ΔH and changes which side the climb starts from.
The sign is right, but the reverse climb starts at the products, 38 kJ, not at the reactants.
Right: going backward climbs from 38 kJ to 214 kJ, then ends at 125 kJ, higher than it started.
The reverse reaction passes over the same hump; climbing it from 38 kJ to 214 kJ takes 176 kJ/mol.

items.q: A catalyst is added to the reaction mixture. How does the diagram change?
options: The peak is lower, and the products move down, so ΔH becomes more negative.
The peak stays the same, and the products move down, so more energy is released.
The peak is higher, so the reaction absorbs extra energy and ΔH becomes positive.
The peak is lower; the reactant and product levels, and so ΔH, stay the same.

why.correct: ΔH depends only on where the reactants and products sit. A catalyst lowers the hump between them.
options: The products are the same substances, so their enthalpy is unchanged.
A catalyst changes the path, which is the peak, not the end points.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy; it does not raise it, and it does not change ΔH.
Right: a catalyst offers a path with a lower activation energy but starts and ends at the same substances.

items.q: Which reactions are endothermic? Select all that apply.
options: Reaction P
Reaction Q
Reaction R
Reaction S

why.correct: An endothermic reaction ends higher than it starts: products above reactants, ΔH > 0. The height of the hump does not decide this.
options: Products at 110 kJ are above reactants at 50 kJ: ΔH = +60 kJ/mol.
Products at 20 kJ are below reactants at 80 kJ: ΔH = −60 kJ/mol, exothermic.
Products at 95 kJ are above reactants at 30 kJ: ΔH = +65 kJ/mol.
Products at 70 kJ are below reactants at 90 kJ: ΔH = −20 kJ/mol, exothermic.

items.q: Which reaction has the largest activation energy in the forward direction?
options: Reaction P, with the largest increase in enthalpy overall
Reaction R, with a climb of 130 kJ/mol
Reaction S, because its hump is at 150 kJ
Reaction Q, because it releases the most energy

why.correct: Ea(forward) = top − reactants: P 95, Q 40, R 130, S 60 kJ/mol. The largest is R.
options: P's overall rise is 60 kJ/mol and its climb is 95 kJ/mol; R climbs further.
Right: 160 − 30 = 130 kJ/mol, the largest climb from reactants to the top.
S starts at 90 kJ, so its climb is only 60 kJ/mol. The climb, not the height, is Ea.
Releasing energy is about ΔH; Q's climb is just 40 kJ/mol.

items.q: Reactions P and Q have the same size of ΔH. What does the diagram data show about them?
options: Both release 60 kJ per mole of reaction, because the size of ΔH is the same.
Both absorb 60 kJ per mole of reaction, because each hump is above its reactants.
P absorbs 60 kJ per mole of reaction and Q releases 60 kJ, so their signs are opposite.
They have the same activation energy, because they have the same size of ΔH.

why.correct: ΔH(P) = 110 − 50 = +60 kJ/mol; ΔH(Q) = 20 − 80 = −60 kJ/mol. Equal sizes, opposite directions of energy flow.
options: Same size, but P's products are higher than its reactants, so P absorbs energy.
Every hump is above its reactants; the hump sets Ea, while the end points set ΔH.
Right: P ends 60 kJ higher (+60) and Q ends 60 kJ lower (−60).
Ea and ΔH are separate: P climbs 95 kJ/mol and Q climbs 40 kJ/mol.

items.q: Determine the activation energy, in kJ/mol, of the reverse of Reaction R (products → reactants).

mistakes.why: Value: that is the forward activation energy, measured from the reactants. The reverse climb starts at the products.
Value: you read the height of the hump. The activation energy is the climb from the starting level up to the hump.

why.correct: Ea(reverse) = top of the hump − products = 160 kJ − 95 kJ = 65 kJ/mol.

items.q: On an energy diagram, where is ΔH of a reaction shown?
options: As the vertical distance from the reactant level to the product level
As the vertical distance from the reactant level to the top of the hump
As the horizontal length of the curve from start to finish
As the height of the top of the hump above the axis

why.correct: Energies on the diagram are vertical differences. The difference between the two flat ends is ΔH.
options: Right: ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants).
That distance is the forward activation energy.
The horizontal axis shows progress of the reaction, not energy.
The peak's height alone is neither ΔH nor Ea; energies are differences between levels.

items.q: A diagram for the reaction 2 H₂O₂(aq) → 2 H₂O(l) + O₂(g), which warms the solution, is drawn by a student with the products higher than the reactants. What is wrong?
options: The products belong at the same level as the reactants, because atoms are conserved.
A reaction that warms its surroundings releases energy, so its products belong below the reactants.
Nothing is wrong, because a reaction that warms its surroundings gains enthalpy.
The hump is missing, because a reaction that releases energy has no activation energy.

why.correct: The diagram shows the system. An exothermic system ends with less enthalpy, so the products sit below the reactants.
options: Atoms are conserved, but energy is not stored the same way in different bonds; the levels differ.
Right: warming the solution means the system lost energy, so ΔH < 0 and the products sit lower.
The surroundings gain energy; the system, whose enthalpy is drawn, loses it.
The student's hump is not the issue, and exothermic reactions do have activation energies.

items.q: Which energy diagram matches an endothermic reaction that is fast at room temperature?
options: Products well below the reactants, with a small hump
Products a little above the reactants, with a very tall hump
Products a little above the reactants, with a small hump
Products level with the reactants, with no hump

why.correct: Two separate readings: the end levels give the sign of ΔH; the hump gives the activation energy, which governs speed (5.6).
options: A small hump fits a fast reaction, but products below reactants make it exothermic.
Endothermic is right, but a tall hump means a large Ea and a slow reaction.
Right: products above reactants means endothermic; a small hump means a small Ea and a fast reaction.
Level ends give ΔH = 0, and a reaction that rearranges bonds has a hump.

items.q: A reaction has ΔH = −45 kJ/mol and a forward activation energy of 70 kJ/mol. The reaction is run backward instead. Predict how each value compares with the forward reaction.

variables.name: Size of ΔH
variables.why: The same two levels are compared, so the size, 45 kJ/mol, is unchanged; only the sign flips.

variables.name: Activation energy
variables.why: The reverse climb starts from the lower product level: 70 + 45 = 115 kJ/mol.

variables.name: Enthalpy of the starting substances
variables.why: The reverse reaction starts at the products, which sit 45 kJ lower than the forward reactants.

why.correct: Reading a diagram backward: same levels, same hump; ΔH flips sign, and Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) − ΔH = 70 − (−45) = 115 kJ/mol.

items.q: Methane burns in oxygen with ΔH = −890 kJ/mol, yet a gas stove does not light until a spark is applied. Which energy diagram explains both facts?
options: Products far below reactants, with a hump that the spark helps the molecules climb
Products far above reactants, so the spark supplies the extra energy stored in the products
Products far below reactants, with no hump, so the spark is not really needed
Products level with reactants, with a hump that the spark climbs

why.correct: ΔH (end levels) tells how much energy is released; Ea (the hump) tells whether molecules have enough energy to start. Once burning, the energy released keeps lighting new molecules.
options: Right: the low products make it strongly exothermic; the hump (Ea) is why it needs a start.
A ΔH of −890 kJ/mol means the products are far below the reactants.
Without a hump, methane would burn the moment it met air; the spark is needed.
Level ends would mean ΔH = 0, not −890 kJ/mol.

items.q: Which pair of quantities can be read from an energy diagram without any other data?
options: The sign of ΔH and the temperature at which the reaction is run
The sign of ΔH and whether the forward Ea is larger than the reverse Ea
The rate constant and the time the reaction takes to finish
The mass of products formed and the mass of reactants used

why.correct: An energy diagram gives enthalpy levels: the sign and size of ΔH and both activation energies. For an exothermic reaction, the reverse Ea is the larger one.
options: Temperature is not on the diagram; its axes are enthalpy and progress of the reaction.
Right: both follow from where the ends sit relative to each other and to the hump.
The diagram gives Ea but not a rate constant or a time; those need more data.
Masses come from stoichiometry, not from an energy diagram.

items.q: For an exothermic elementary reaction, how do the forward and reverse activation energies compare?
options: The forward Ea is larger, by the size of ΔH
They are equal, because both directions pass over the same hump
The reverse Ea is larger, by the size of ΔH
The reverse Ea is zero, because the reverse reaction absorbs energy

why.correct: Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) − ΔH. With ΔH negative, Ea(reverse) is larger.
options: That is true for an endothermic reaction, where the reactants are lower.
Same hump, different starting levels, so different climbs.
Right: the reverse climb starts from the lower product level, so it is longer by |ΔH|.
The reverse still has to climb the hump; its Ea is the larger of the two.
